An island of Irish legend said to rise from the sea west of Ireland once every seven years, drawn on charts from 1325 until the 1800s. Never found.
The island the monk Brendan is said to have reached on his voyage; in the Canaries it is San Borondón, sighted west of La Palma and never found.
A phantom island south of Iceland on the Zeno map of 1558, copied onto many charts for over a century.
Reported by one of Frobisher's ships in 1578, searched for until the 1800s and then said to have sunk: "the Sunken Land of Buss".
An island of 16th century charts off Newfoundland, said to be full of wailing spirits; perhaps a real island with a grim story attached.

properties.n: Antillia, the Isle of Seven Cities (legend)
properties.d: A great rectangular island on 15th century Atlantic charts, said to be settled by seven bishops fleeing Iberia.
Plato's island beyond the Pillars of Hercules, sunk in a single day and night. A story, not a place: lettered here in a cartouche as old maps did.
The whirlpool in the Gulf of Corryvreckan between Jura and Scarba, where the flood tide runs over a pinnacle of rock; one of the largest in the world.
The tidal whirlpools off the tip of Lofoten, written up by Olaus Magnus and later by Poe and Verne as the Maelstrom.
The whirling currents of the Strait of Messina, the Charybdis of the Odyssey, opposite the rock of Scylla.
One of the strongest tidal currents in the world, near Bodø, with whirlpools up to 10 m across.
Tidal whirlpools in the Naruto Strait between Shikoku and Awaji, painted by Hiroshige.
The largest whirlpool in the western hemisphere, in the channel between Deer Island, New Brunswick, and Eastport, Maine.
The phantom ship of legend doomed to sail for ever off the Cape of Good Hope; a sighting is said to bring bad luck.
Found drifting with no one aboard between the Azores and Portugal in 1872; the crew were never found. (Wikidata places her wreck elsewhere: she was later lost off Haiti.)
Said to have run on to the Goodwin Sands in 1748 and to return every fifty years; a legend without a record.
The glowing ghost ship of Chiloé folklore, crewed by the drowned.
A cargo steamer abandoned in the ice off Alaska in 1931 and sighted drifting for decades after.
A burning ship said to appear off Block Island, Rhode Island, after a wreck of 1738.
A schooner found aground on Diamond Shoals, North Carolina, in 1921 with no one aboard.
Cornish legend: a mermaid who lured the chorister Mathey Trewella into the sea at Pendour Cove; she is carved on a bench end in Zennor church.
Cornish legend: a mermaid shot at by a local man cursed the harbour, and the Doom Bar sandbank rose across its mouth.
Hans Christian Andersen's tale of 1837; Edvard Eriksen's statue has sat on her rock in Copenhagen harbour since 1913.
A rock above the narrowest bend of the Rhine, where a siren combing her golden hair lured boatmen to their wreck (Brentano, Heine).
Syrenka, the mermaid of the Vistula who swore to defend the city; she has been on its arms since the 1300s.
A small mermaid said to have been found on the shore of Benbecula in 1830 and given a burial at Nunton.
The rocky islets off Positano known since antiquity as the Sirenuse, the islands of the sirens.
The sea monster of Norwegian fishermen's tales, described by Bishop Erik Pontoppidan in his Natural History of Norway (1752 to 1753) as an island-sized beast off this coast.
A great sandbank in the North Sea, fished for cod and herring since the Middle Ages; the Dutch "dogger" boats gave it its name.
Shallow banks where the Labrador Current meets the Gulf Stream; Basque, Portuguese, French and English fleets fished their cod from the 1500s.
A rich bank east of Cape Cod, fished by New England schooners for centuries.
An outlying bank east of the Grand Banks, fished for cod and redfish.
A bank round the lonely rock of Rockall, fished for haddock.
Every winter the skrei, the spawning Arctic cod, come to the Vestfjord; fished here for over a thousand years and dried as stockfish.
A large bank in the middle of the North Sea.
The broad shelf south of Africa, fished for hake and sardine.
Spawning grounds of Icelandic cod off the south-west coast.
One of the Scotian Shelf banks, fished for cod and haddock.
The cold, rich Humboldt Current waters off Peru, one of the most productive fisheries on Earth.
Cod and haddock grounds round Bjørnøya in the Barents Sea.

The island off Hispaniola used by buccaneers in the 1600s.
The buccaneers' harbour of Jamaica, much of which sank in the earthquake of 1692.
The corsairs of Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli and Salé raided shipping and coasts as far as Iceland from the 1500s to the 1800s.
A haven of pirates of the Indian Ocean in the late 1600s and early 1700s.
A narrow sea lane where piracy has been reported for centuries, and still is.
